name: Phase Two: Choose the Pilot
title: Phase Two: Choose the Pilot
answer: Phase Two of Pilot, Measure, Scale is about choosing the first pilot by starting with a clear problem rather than a product. The pilot should be low in risk and high in visibility, so the school can build habits and trust before trying harder tools. This matters because starting with a product often creates a solution looking for a problem.

sections.body: The idea is to define the problem before looking at tools. A school might focus on the time teachers spend writing parent messages, ninth graders failing algebra at an alarming rate, or too much food thrown away in the cafeteria. Once the problem is clear, the district can look for tools that address it and ignore the ones that do not. This solves the common failure of buying a product first and then searching for a use. It keeps the pilot tied to a real need rather than a demo.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In practice, early pilots should be low in risk and high in visibility. Good first choices include drafting tools for teachers, translation for routine family messages, and practice tools with teacher oversight. The text gives ninth grade algebra as an example of a problem that might start a pilot, but it does not set out separate steps for other grade bands. Tools that flag students, score work for grades, or collect sensitive data should wait until the district has run a few simpler pilots well. Success with a small, safe pilot builds the habits and trust that a harder pilot will need.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text does not give an evidence label or report a study finding for this idea. It says researchers have proposed frameworks for judging educational AI on responsibility as well as performance, including accuracy, fairness, transparency, and data protection (Lin et al., 2026). It also says Figure 4.4 lists the evidence and privacy criteria a vendor should be able to answer in writing. Beyond that proposed framework and figure, the idea rests on practice rather than research.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The text sets clear limits on what should come first. Tools that flag students, score work for grades, or collect sensitive data should wait until simpler pilots have been run well. Vendors should be judged on evidence and privacy, not on the demo. A district does not need a formal framework to ask basic questions, but it should require written answers on evidence and privacy criteria. Teacher oversight remains part of practice tools, and the text does not say those decisions leave the school.
